name: Best Orientation and Window Choices for ADUs and Additions in Los Angeles Microclimates

mainEntity.name: How do Los Angeles microclimates and sun exposure affect the best orientation and window choices for an ADU or room addition?
mainEntity.text: How do Los Angeles microclimates and sun exposure affect the best orientation and window choices for an ADU or room addition?

acceptedAnswer.text: Los Angeles has distinct microclimates—from hot valley neighborhoods to cooler coastal zones—and these should shape how you design and glaze an ADU or room addition. In **hot inland areas**, large west- and southwest-facing windows can cause overheating and higher cooling bills. For these sides, prioritize smaller openings, low solar heat gain coefficient (SHGC) glass, and external shading like overhangs or screens. North-facing windows provide softer light with minimal heat gain, making them ideal for studios or home offices. In **coastal or cooler microclimates**, you can more safely use larger south-facing glazing to bring in winter sun, as long as you still consider summer shading. High-quality double-pane windows with low-E coatings are important across microclimates to manage both heat and noise. Orientation also affects **privacy and usability**: placing windows to overlook yards rather than neighboring windows can reduce conflicts, especially when adding a second story or ADU near property lines. Discuss local sun patterns, summer temperatures, and typical breezes for your specific neighborhood with your designer or contractor. Combining this with energy code requirements helps you choose window sizes, types, and placements that keep interior spaces bright without creating hot, uncomfortable rooms.
acceptedAnswer.description: Orientation and microclimate influence overheating and lighting. In hot, sunny areas of Los Angeles, limit large west-facing glass, select low-solar-gain windows, and design shading. In cooler or coastal areas, capture south light with insulated glazing. Window placement should balance daylight, privacy, and energy performance.
